item.title: People open umbrellas when it rains
item.description:
Today the city gets weather, and the people in it notice.

Dressed for the day

Each city now has a climate of its own. The day has four weather blocks, with a temperature that rises and falls, and snow and puddles on the ground. The sound follows too. Birds go quiet in heavy rain.

The people on your street react. Shorts become trousers in the cold, and a coat comes out when it freezes. Not everyone feels the cold in the same way, so two neighbours can dress differently on the same morning. In rain, people open an umbrella or pull up a hood.

item.title: Estates get lawns and benches, and corners get street signs
item.description:
Three changes you can see today. One kerb corner gave us trouble.

Estates with grass, trees and benches

The big estates of slabs and towers now sit in open green land. We add lawns, paths and trees in loose groups. Benches stand along the paths.

Slab and tower doors get a glass canopy. The slabs and towers get balconies. Tall buildings show a lift room and roof equipment on top.

item.title: Street signs, hats and green gardens
item.description:
Today we can tell you where you are. Street names now appear on signs at the corners of junctions.

Names on the corners

Each street gets one sign per corner, and signs never overlap each other. Walk to a junction and look up. You know which street you are on.

Why it matters: on foot you decide at every corner. A sign helps you choose, and you do not need a map. Short blocks give you many corners, so a name on each one is useful.

item.title: Why the game is called Human Scale
item.description:
The game is named after an idea from city planning. “Human scale” means building cities for a person on foot, not for a car. This post explains the idea, and how it shapes every city you will walk through in the game.

A city at 5 km/h

The Danish architect Jan Gehl spent his life watching how people use streets. His main lesson is simple. We walk at about 5 km/h, and our senses are made for that speed. At walking pace we see faces, read shop windows, hear a conversation and notice a door that is open. Many modern streets are designed for cars at 50 or 60 km/h. At that speed, details blur, so the buildings get big and plain, and the street becomes a place you pass through, not a place you are in.

item.title: Neighbourhoods get their own character
item.description:
Hello, and welcome. Human Scale is a top-down pixel-art game about arriving in a new city and building a life there: a room, a job, people you meet, one street at a time. The cities are made for walking.

On evenings when something changed, we post a short note here. On Sundays, we write a longer one. The picture at the top is always the same street, so you can watch it change.

item.title: About this blog
item.description:
Human Scale is a game about arriving in a new city and building a life there: finding a room, a job and people you like, one street at a time.

This blog follows the game while we make it. A short post comes out on days when something changed that you could see or feel in the city, and a longer one sums up the week on Sundays.

How the posts are written. AI helps us write the posts from the studio’s daily notes, and every post is checked before it goes out. The pictures are screenshots, maps and art sheets from our own work. A picture made with AI is marked “AI-made”.
